Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody shares what they have or haven’t watched. Never shame. If a student mentions an adult or much older person sending sexual content, that goes to a counselor the same day.

Every student in the room

Some students were raised to believe porn is wrong and carry heavy guilt, some LGBTQ+ students first saw people like them there, and porn sells stereotypes about race and bodies; leave room for all of them without shame.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why porn pulls so hard, how it works like pro wrestling (real bodies, staged show), how it can become a sexual script when nobody else offers one, and what real intimacy takes instead. The tone stays shame-free. Nobody shares what they watch, and students who've never seen any are welcome too.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start
  2. 5 minHow common, and why it pulls
  3. 7 minReal bodies, staged show, and the script problem
  4. 8 minAgree or disagree, one per slide
  5. 8 minWhat real intimacy takes: turn and talk, share out
  6. 8 minThree moments: at lunch, someone you’re seeing, late nights
  7. 6 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

How common and why, the staged show, the script problem, what real intimacy takes, and one of the three moments.

Before you teach
Keep it shame-free.

Seeing it doesn't make anyone gross or broken. Shame makes a habit harder to change and shuts down the room. Say early: "Most people didn't plan the first time they saw it."

Nobody shares what they watch.

Every question is about "people our age." The four-corners activity asks for opinions about research, never experiences.

Let the laughter pass.

Nervous laughter is normal at the start. Don't scold it. Keep your own tone matter-of-fact and it settles.

Be clear about choking.

This is the one safety fact you say twice: pressure on the neck can cut off blood to the brain within seconds, and there's no safe way to do it. If someone does it without asking, that's not okay, and students can tell someone.

If a student discloses.

An adult who showed a student porn or sent sexual content, or someone who hurt them, is something you can't keep private. Thank them and walk them to a counselor that day.

Be honest about what's debated.

Researchers still argue about "porn addiction" and about the aggression link. Saying so makes the solid findings more believable.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Faith and guilt.

Students raised to believe porn is wrong may feel addicted even after watching fairly little, because the conflict itself feels like losing control. A counselor or a trusted faith leader can help them sort it out without treating them as bad.

LGBTQ+ students.

Porn may have been one of the few places some LGBTQ+ students saw anyone like them. That makes sense. Real queer relationships take the same things everyone's do. Keep every example open to any couple.

Race and stereotypes.

Over half of teens who'd seen porn saw Black people shown in stereotyped ways, and around half saw the same for Latino and Asian people. If a student has felt reduced to a stereotype, say plainly that it comes from the script and says nothing true about them.

Family conversations.

Some families talk openly, some never do, some have clear faith rules. The question "which adult could you ask?" lets each student pick someone who fits their family: a parent, an older cousin, a doctor, a counselor.

Bodies.

Performers are cast, lit and edited. Students of every body type, including students with disabilities, should hear that comparing to porn is comparing to a casting call.

Students who've never seen it.

Say they're welcome and normal. The lesson still helps them understand what classmates are absorbing.

What the research says

Nearly three out of four teens had seen porn online, and the average age of first exposure was 12. More had seen it by accident than on purpose. Only 27% said it shows how most people have sex.

Robb and Mann, Common Sense Media, 2023

More teens said they'd learned a lot about sex from a parent, caregiver or trusted adult (47%) than from porn (27%). Only 33% of teens who'd seen porn had ever seen anyone ask for consent.

Robb and Mann, Common Sense Media, 2023

Among 14 to 17 year olds, parents and friends topped the list of helpful sources and about 8% named porn. By the early twenties, porn became the most-named source.

Rothman et al., Archives of Sexual Behavior, 2021

About 1 in 5 adult women said a partner had choked them during sex, and people who watched porn more often were more likely to report it.

Herbenick et al., Journal of Sexual Medicine, 2020

Twenty years of studies link teen porn use with more stereotyped beliefs about gender and more permissive attitudes about sex. Most were snapshots, so they can't prove cause.

Peter and Valkenburg, Journal of Sex Research, 2016

People who believe porn is wrong often feel addicted even when they watch fairly little.

Grubbs et al., Archives of Sexual Behavior, 2019

Across 93 studies, couples who talk about sex well are more satisfied with their sex lives and relationships.

Mallory, Journal of Family Psychology, 2022
